B1:
Touched fires many times: once for each body part (feet, legs and so on) and repeatedly as the contact jitters. Several of these events arrive before part:Destroy() takes effect, or are already queued (especially with deferred signals), so each one awards 10 coins.

Fix it with a debounce or a consumed flag that is set before granting:
```lua
local part = script.Parent
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local collected = false
part.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    if collected then return end
    local plr = Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter(hit.Parent)
    if not plr then return end
    collected = true
    part:Destroy()
    plr.leaderstats.Coins.Value += 10
end)
```
For respawning or per-player pickups, track it per player with a table such as `claimed[plr] = true`, with a cooldown. Do this on the server.
B2:
With StreamingEnabled on, the client only has instances near the player. Distant parts of the map, like that Hotel Door, haven't streamed in yet, or have streamed out, when the LocalScript runs. Dot-indexing a missing child then errors.

Fix 1: wait for it to stream in and handle stream-out. Use `workspace.Map.Buildings:WaitForChild("Hotel"):WaitForChild("Door")` (with a timeout and nil check), and set the Hotel/Door model's ModelStreamingMode = Atomic so its parts arrive together. Reconnect if it is removed and comes back.

Fix 2 (best for many doors): tag doors with CollectionService ("Door") and use `CollectionService:GetInstanceAddedSignal("Door")` plus GetTagged to connect Touched as each door streams in, disconnecting on GetInstanceRemovedSignal.

Alternatively, handle Touched on the server, where everything exists. Making the door Persistent also works but costs client memory, so use it sparingly.
B3:
Bugs:
1. It always returns PurchaseGranted, even when pcall failed, so the player is charged and gets nothing.
2. There is no PurchaseId idempotency. If the callback is retried after a crash, or the receipt is re-delivered, the player gets double coins.
3. It uses non-atomic GetAsync + SetAsync read-modify-write, which races with other servers or saves and can lose or duplicate coins.
4. It doesn't handle the player having left. plr can be nil, which errors on plr.UserId, and the coins aren't reflected in the live session data. It also ignores ProductId.

Corrected behavior:
- If the player isn't in the server, return NotProcessedYet.
- Look up the handler by ProductId.
- In one UpdateAsync on the player's key (or the session-locked profile), check whether info.PurchaseId is already in the processed list. If it isn't, add 100 coins and record the PurchaseId (keeping a capped list).
- If the save succeeded, return PurchaseGranted. If the pcall failed, return NotProcessedYet so Roblox retries.
- Update the in-memory or session data from the same result so there are no overwrites.
B4:
Remotes serialize arguments. Metatables aren't sent, so the client receives a plain table {Name="Rifle", Ammo=30} with no __index, and w:Fire() is nil. Functions are never transmitted either. Instances are sent as references, and the client can only resolve an instance that exists in its replicated view. ServerStorage never replicates to clients, so the Muzzle reference arrives as nil.

Fix:
- Send plain data, such as an id or state table, and rebuild the object on the client. For example, `setmetatable(data, WeaponClient)` using a shared module in ReplicatedStorage, or look it up by name or id.
- For the part, move the Muzzle (or a clone) to ReplicatedStorage or Workspace before firing, or send the data the client needs (CFrame, asset name) instead. With streaming, also make sure it is streamed in.
- Keep authoritative logic like ammo on the server.
B5:
workspace:Raycast's second argument is the direction vector, and its length is the ray's range. `(target - origin).Unit` has length 1, so the ray only travels 1 stud and almost never reaches anything. It also lacks RaycastParams, so it can hit the shooter's own character.

Fix:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local MAX = 300
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * MAX -- or (target - origin) for exact distance
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
Guard against target == origin, which gives a NaN unit vector.
B6:
When the last player leaves, the server starts shutting down. PlayerRemoving fires, but the server can close before the yielding SetAsync finishes, because nothing keeps it alive. Closing Studio or a shutdown can also skip PlayerRemoving entirely.

The standard fix is game:BindToClose. On close, save every remaining player's data in parallel (task.spawn per player) and wait until all saves finish. BindToClose gives you up to about 30 seconds. Track which players have already been saved by PlayerRemoving so you don't double-save. Use UpdateAsync with session locking, pcall and retries. Add periodic autosaves (staggered, dirty-only) so a crash loses at most a minute of progress.

```lua
game:BindToClose(function()
  local pending = 0
  for _, p in Players:GetPlayers() do
    pending += 1
    task.spawn(function() savePlayer(p, true); pending -= 1 end)
  end
  while pending > 0 do task.wait() end
end)
```

```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local UseAbility = game.ReplicatedStorage.Remotes.UseAbility
local COOLDOWN = 2
local lastUse = {} -- [Player] = os.clock()

UseAbility.OnServerEvent:Connect(function(player, abilityId)
    if typeof(abilityId) ~= "string" or #abilityId > 32 then return end
    local now = os.clock()
    local last = lastUse[player]
    if last and now - last < COOLDOWN then return end -- spam ignored silently
    lastUse[player] = now
    local char = player.Character
    local hum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end
    performAbility(player, abilityId) -- server-authoritative effect

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
    lastUse[player] = nil -- no leak
end)
```
The cooldown is checked and stamped on the server before any yield. The client can show its own cooldown UI, but the server's check decides.

```lua
local MPS = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local DSS = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local store = DSS:GetDataStore("PlayerData")
local GEMS100 = 123456

local handlers = {
  [GEMS100] = function(data) data.Gems = (data.Gems or 0) + 100 end,
}

MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(info)
  local handler = handlers[info.ProductId]
  if not handler then return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end
  local player = Players:GetPlayerByUserId(info.PlayerId)
  if not player then return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end -- retried when they rejoin

  local granted = false
  local ok, err = pcall(store.UpdateAsync, store, "Player_" .. info.PlayerId, function(data)
    data = data or {}
    data.Receipts = data.Receipts or {}
    if data.Receipts[info.PurchaseId] then
      granted = true
      return nil -- already granted: no write
    end
    handler(data)
    data.Receipts[info.PurchaseId] = os.time() -- prune old entries elsewhere
    granted = true
    return data
  end)
  if not ok or not granted then
    warn("Receipt failed:", err)
    return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet
  end
  -- refresh live session data / leaderstats from the saved value here
  return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
```

```lua
local TweenService = game:GetService("TweenService")
local info = TweenInfo.new(0.4, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)

    end)
    t:Play()
```

Set menu.AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5) so it lands centered. The Completed check keeps a quick reopen from being hidden by an old close tween.
B10:
```lua
local MAX_RANGE = 200
local DAMAGE = 20

local function shoot(player: Player, targetPos: Vector3)
    if typeof(targetPos) ~= "Vector3" or targetPos ~= targetPos then return end
    local char = player.Character
    local head = char and char:FindFirstChild("Head")
    local hum = char and char:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if not head or not hum or hum.Health <= 0 then return end

    local origin = head.Position
    local offset = targetPos - origin
    if offset.Magnitude < 1e-3 then return end
    local dir = offset.Unit * MAX_RANGE

    local params = RaycastParams.new()
    params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
    params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {char}

    local result = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
    if not result then return end
    local model = result.Instance:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
    local targetHum = model and model:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if targetHum and targetHum.Health > 0 then
        targetHum:TakeDamage(DAMAGE)
    end
end
```
When this is called from a remote, also rate-limit by fire rate and check that the weapon is equipped.

```lua
local CollectionService = game:GetService("CollectionService")
local TAG = "KillBrick"

CollectionService:GetInstanceRemovedSignal(TAG):Connect(onRemoved)
```

B13:
(a) Client to server: the client fires a RemoteEvent (or invokes a RemoteFunction, client to server, if the UI needs an immediate success or fail result) with just the itemId. All validation happens on the server: the item exists, the price comes from the server config, the player has enough coins, rate limits, and so on. The coin balance lives in server-side player data and is never trusted from the client. The server deducts the coins and grants the sword atomically.

(b) Server to client: the server pushes the new balance to the client with RemoteEvent:FireClient, or with a replicated value such as leaderstats or an attribute the UI listens to.

Why not RemoteFunction:InvokeClient for the UI update: the server would yield waiting on the client. A malicious or disconnected client can never return, which hangs the server thread forever. It can also error or return garbage that propagates into server code. The server gains nothing by waiting for a UI acknowledgement. Server-to-client communication should be fire-and-forget.
B14:
Teleport data (TeleportOptions:SetTeleportData) is carried through the client. On the destination it can be spoofed, especially when read on the client. Even the server's GetJoinData().TeleportData is only partly trustworthy, it is size-limited, and it is lost if the teleport fails or the player joins another way. That makes it fine for hints like the chosen map, party id or UI state, but never for coin balances.

DataStores are authoritative and persistent. Save the coin balance and loadout to the player's profile, and release the session lock before teleporting. The destination loads the profile with session locking and retries until the lock is released. MemoryStores are fast and short-lived (with TTL). They work well as a match "ticket", such as a reservation with the chosen loadout and match id that the destination validates (membership, SourcePlaceId), with a default-deny fallback.

Choice: keep coins (and owned or equipped loadout) in DataStore with session locking, saved before teleport. Use a MemoryStore ticket or teleport data only for transient match selection, validated on the server against owned items.
B15:
Per-instance Scripts mean about 610 copies of nearly identical code. Each has its own VM thread and memory, startup costs add up, and fixing a bug means editing hundreds of copies or packages that drift apart. They are hard to profile and easy to break with streaming. They also run on the server even when the logic could be shared.

The recommended structure is a tag-driven architecture:
- Tag instances with CollectionService ("Door", "Pickup", "Turret"). Use attributes for per-instance config such as speed, damage or key id.
- One server Script (or a ModuleScript system) per tag. On GetInstanceAddedSignal it builds a component or state object for that instance, and on GetInstanceRemovedSignal it cleans up connections and state.
- Process GetTagged at startup.
- Use shared loops for periodic work, for example a single Heartbeat or a scheduler for all 60 turrets at a throttled rate, instead of 60 loops.
- Newly spawned clones keep their tags, so the added signal handles them automatically.
- On clients with StreamingEnabled, instances that stream in fire the added signal and instances that stream out fire the removed signal, so client-side visuals use the same pattern.
- Keep authoritative logic on the server and cosmetic logic on the client.
B16:
Give network ownership of a car to the driver. Assign it with VehicleSeat or the car's root part SetNetworkOwner(driverPlayer) when they sit, and reset it to the server with SetNetworkOwner(nil) or anchor the car when it is empty or parked. Otherwise physics lags and steering feels bad. Ownership resets when parts are unanchored, so set it again after that.

Security risk: the owning client simulates the car's physics authoritatively. An exploiter can set any position or velocity, which allows speed hacks, teleporting, flying, skipping checkpoints, or flinging other cars.

The server must still validate:
- Sample the car position and velocity at a few Hz and compare against the maximum speed with a margin. Check for hovering or flying and teleport-sized jumps.
- Require checkpoints in order and enforce plausible lap and segment times.
- Compute finish times, race results and rewards on the server.
- Use a strike system before acting. On violation, take ownership back (SetNetworkOwner(nil)) and reset the car to its last good CFrame.
- Whitelist legitimate server boosts.

The 2026 Server Authority mode is an alternative, but test it for high-speed vehicles first.
B17:
Use an UnreliableRemoteEvent for the continuous aim and position stream. It is unordered and best-effort, so packets can be dropped or arrive out of order. It doesn't retry or queue behind lost packets, which is ideal for state that is overwritten every tick. Payloads over about 1,000 bytes are dropped, and client-to-server request rate is throttled.

Handling the constraints:
- Send compact data, such as a quantized direction (yaw and pitch as numbers, or buffer-packed) rather than full CFrames.
- Send at 10-20 Hz or only when the value changes meaningfully, instead of every frame.
- Include a sequence number or timestamp and ignore stale or out-of-order packets on the server.
- Interpolate on receivers.
- Never use it for discrete, must-arrive events such as fire, reload or equip start and stop. Use a reliable RemoteEvent for those, otherwise effects get stuck on.
- Validate and rate-limit on the server: clamp the values and reject NaN.
- The server can often derive position itself from the replicated character, so you may not need to send it at all.
B18:
Split the NPCs across a pool of Actors, for example 8-32 Actors, each handling a slice of NPCs. Don't use one Actor per NPC, and don't put everything under one Actor, because scripts in the same Actor run serially. Inside each Actor:
- Use RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize()) to do the read-only work in parallel: workspace:Raycast, distance and path scoring, choosing targets.
- Store the results in local tables.
- Call task.synchronize() and apply the writes serially: setting CFrames, MoveTo, firing events, changing properties.
Stagger the NPC "brains" to around 5-10 Hz instead of every frame. Profile in the MicroProfiler before and after.

Limitations:
- In parallel phases you can't write most instance properties, create or destroy instances, or call most yielding or non-thread-safe APIs. Check each API's thread-safety label.
- require isn't allowed while desynchronized.
- Each Actor gets its own copy of ModuleScripts, so state isn't shared. Use SharedTable (with atomic increment/update) or Actor messaging (SendMessage, BindToMessageParallel).
- There is overhead in syncing and in message passing.
- The work must be chunky enough to pay off.
- PathfindingService:ComputeAsync isn't parallel-safe, so keep it serial and throttled.
B19:
Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. Configure it in Studio Properties, not from scripts.
- StreamingMinRadius: the default is 64. Raise it modestly (for example 64-128) if gameplay needs nearby certainty.
- StreamingTargetRadius: the default is 1024. Lower it for big or dense worlds, for example 256-512 on mobile-heavy games. It must be greater than MinRadius.
- StreamOutBehavior = Opportunistic, so memory is reclaimed proactively instead of only when memory is low.
- StreamingIntegrityMode = PauseOutsideLoadedArea (or MinimumRadiusPause) to avoid falling through unloaded ground.
- ModelStreamingBehavior = Improved.
- Set the ModelStreamingMode of important or interactable models to Atomic, so they stream as a whole unit. Use Persistent only for the few models every client must always have, because it costs memory.
- Use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync before teleporting a player across the map.

Fix scripts that assumed everything is loaded:
- Replace direct dot-paths with WaitForChild (with a timeout and nil checks).
- Use CollectionService tags with added and removed signals.
- Don't cache references to parts that can stream out.
- Handle stream-out by disconnecting.
- Keep authoritative logic on the server, where everything exists.

Test on a low-end phone.
B20:
The write budget for the whole experience is 300 + 20 x CCU per minute, shared by all servers and Open Cloud (since 2026). Per-server limits are about 60 + 40 x players per minute. 80 players saving every 5 seconds is 960 writes per minute from one server. That uses most of the server's budget before you count PlayerRemoving saves, purchases or retries. All of them fire on the same tick, so they burst. The request queue (about 30 per type) fills up, and you get 30x "queue full" or throttle errors (302) that drop saves. Per-key rate limits and same-key overlap also cause conflicts.

Better design:
- Keep data in memory (session-locked profiles). Autosave each profile every 60-120 seconds, staggered with random offsets, and only if it changed (dirty flag).
- Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose.
- Save immediately only for important events, such as purchases, which are tracked by PurchaseId.
- Use UpdateAsync with pcall and exponential backoff with jitter.
- Check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving, and defer saves when the budget is low.
- Never retry in tight loops.

B22:
The Input Action System has three instance types:
- InputContext: groups actions. It has Enabled, Priority and Sink properties.
- InputAction: one game mechanic, such as Jump or Sprint. Its Type is Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D or ViewportPosition.
- InputBinding: maps one piece of hardware to an action, using KeyCode (keyboard or gamepad), UIButton (a touch GUI button), or composite or modifier keys.

Signaling a press: for Bool actions, the InputAction fires Pressed and Released. For all types, StateChanged fires with the new value. You can also poll with InputAction:GetState().

Menu precedence: put the menu's actions in an InputContext with a higher Priority than the gameplay or default player-script contexts, and set Sink = true. That context then consumes those inputs and lower-priority contexts don't receive them. Toggle it with Enabled while the menu is open. This matters now that the default PlayerScripts run on IAS (Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem). Also reset held states, such as sprint, when the menu context takes over, so released inputs aren't lost.
B23:
It is Roblox's engine UI styling system, which works like CSS for GuiObjects. The main instances are:
- StyleSheet: a container of rules, and it can also hold tokens.
- StyleRule: a Selector string plus property values set with SetProperties. Rules can be nested.
- StyleDerive: makes one sheet inherit from or extend another, for example a theme sheet deriving base rules.
- StyleLink: attached to a ScreenGui or other UI root, it links a StyleSheet so its rules apply to that subtree.
- StyleQuery: conditional rules, for example by screen size or preferred input.

Selectors can match class names (Frame, TextButton), tags (.Tag, from CollectionService), names (#Name), GuiState pseudo-states (:hover, :pressed) and descendant or child relationships.

How styles reach the UI: the StyleLink connects a sheet to the instance tree. Matching rules then set properties on matching descendants, with specificity and order resolving conflicts.

Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (for example Primary = Color3, CornerRadius = UDim) and reference them in rules as "$Primary". To swap themes at runtime, point StyleDerive or StyleLink at another sheet with the same token names.

Avoid setting the same property from both scripts and styles.
B24:
The check uses facial age estimation, done through the Roblox app with the camera and processed by a vendor (Persona). Users 13+ can verify with an ID instead. It was required for chat starting in late 2025 in some regions, and globally from January 2026.

Users are placed into age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20 and 21+.

By default, users can chat only with people in their own age group and the adjacent groups. For example, a 13-15 user can chat with 9-12, 13-15 and 16-17, but not with adults. Under-9s have chat off by default and need parental consent. Trusted Connections, for verified users 13+ who know each other, allow chat across wider age groups. Users who haven't done the check can't use chat.

For developers:
- All player text must go through TextChatService. A custom RemoteEvent chat would bypass filtering and the age rules.
- Use TextChatService:CanUsersChatAsync and CanUsersDirectChatAsync (and GetChatGroupsAsync) before creating private channels.
- There is no age API, so don't build gameplay that depends on chat.
